newsitem.title: south africa: FEATURE-THIRSTY WORLD CLAMOURS FOR S.AFRICAN WINE.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-THIRSTY WORLD CLAMOURS FOR S.AFRICAN WINE.

text.p: In the wine lands of South Africa the vines are coming into leaf and farmers are smiling, basking in the new-found popularity of their once-shunned product.
In the dark days of apartheid no respectable dinner table would field a South African label, and trade boycotts left a vast lake of surplus wine.
But two and a half years on from the first free elections, the world is clamouring for all the quality wine the country can produce, and the lake has run dry.

This year exports are on track to break all records at 10 million cases, up 30 percent on the 7.7 million shipped in 1995, Kobus van Niekerk, managing director of the main export agency KWV International, told Reuters.
Yet despite a 1,000 percent surge in overseas sales since 1993, the international market's thirst for South African wines remains unsated.
For growers, some of whom faced bankruptcy a few years ago, South Africa's re-entry into the world community, coupled with the windfall of a weak rand, has spelt salvation.
But the sudden superstar status in the wine world has brought problems too, as the industry struggles to keep up with its success on supermarket shelves from New York to Tokyo.

"We do have a problem in supplying demand which is likely to be with us for another two years or so -- especially on the red wine side -- since the industry cannot adapt that quickly,'' said van Niekerk.
With annual production running at more than one billion litres a year, South Africa is no lightweight when it comes to producing wine, ranking among the world's top 10 producers.
The trouble is it is growing the wrong sort of grapes for its new international clientele.
The world wants South African red, but 80 percent of the crop is actually white. Furthermore, very little of the harvest is made up of the classic grape varieties most in demand.
As a result there is a chronic shortage of premium cultivars, notably Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot, Pinotage, Shiraz, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.
The problem is most acute in the case of Pinotage, a unique South African cross of Pinot Noir and Cinsaut, which was first created in 1925 but has long been sidelined by the wine trade.
In the last two years, however, Pinotage has enjoyed a remarkable renaissance as wineries experimented with a completely different style for the grape which has taken the world by storm.
Unfortunately, after years of grubbing out Pinotage vines, the supply is simply not there, and the only true South African variety makes up a meagre three percent of the national crop.

Nurseries are working overtime to supply growers with rootstock of the more fashionable varieties, in preference to the predominantly white grapes used to supply the local market with semi-sweet whites, fortified wines and brandy.
At the same time, new winemakers are changing old practices, producing fruitier, easier-drinking wines typical of other New World suppliers, such as Australia, New Zealand and Chile.
John Platter, author of a best-selling guide to South African wine, believes the new wave of producers is making its mark, producing a new style of South African wine more in tune with modern tastes.
"Their technology and approach is really very refreshing,'' he said.

But turning the supertanker around is a slow business and in the meantime South Africa faces complaints from disgruntled buyers who argue it has stretched itself too thin in its rush to supply some 55 different markets around the world.
Van Niekerk accepts the criticism and says in future his organisation, representing 4,700 growers, aims to focus on key markets such as Britain, continental Europe, the United States and Japan.

KWV, a giant co-operative of growers in the heart of the winelands, also hopes to instil a more market-orientated and adaptable approach among its members by converting into a company, linking farmers direct to the profit motive via dividend payments.
Details of the plan to unbundle the group's assets to its 4,700 members and form a new company were unveiled earlier this month and, if approved, will be implemented by next April.
